props.title: West Side Story
props.initialSlug: Modern Romeo and Juliet tale between rival NYC gangs

sections.content: West Side Story (1961) revolutionized the movie musical through Jerome Robbins' electric choreography and Leonard Bernstein's sophisticated score. The film transforms Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet into a searing commentary on urban gang violence and racial tensions in 1950s New York. Robert Wise's direction brings unprecedented grit to the genre, while maintaining the theatrical energy that made the stage version explosive. The film's influence echoes through later urban musicals like Fame (1980) and In the Heights (2021), proving that social commentary and spectacular dance numbers can coexist brilliantly.

sections.content: The 2021 Steven Spielberg remake of West Side Story demonstrates the original's lasting impact while addressing its problematic elements. Where the 1961 version used brownface makeup on Rita Moreno and other actors, Spielberg cast actual Latinx performers and incorporated untranslated Spanish dialogue. Both versions showcase how dance can express tribal tension and romantic yearning, but through different visual languages - Robbins' balletic style versus Justin Peck's grittier, street-influenced choreography.

The film's innovative fusion of classical and jazz music influenced countless subsequent musicals. Chicago (2002) borrowed its knife-fight dance sequence staging, while La La Land (2016) paid direct homage to the rooftop dance sequences. The "Tonight" quintet remains one of cinema's most complex musical numbers, weaving multiple character perspectives into a unified dramatic crescendo that films like Les Misérables (2012) have tried to replicate. sections.content: West Side Story transformed how violence could be portrayed through dance on screen. The prologue's finger-snapping tension and the explosive "Cool" number created a new vocabulary for expressing aggression through movement. Later films like Grease (1978) and Fame (1980) built on this foundation, while modern musicals like Moulin Rouge! (2001) continue drawing from its kinetic camera techniques and color psychology.
